label: React
description: Scenario-based MCQ across five levels: JSX and component fundamentals, hooks and state, performance and error boundaries, state management and testing.

questions.title: While looping over an array of numbers with no unique value, React warns for the unique key. What should be used to remove this warning?
questions.prompt: While looping over an array of numbers with no unique value, React warns for the unique key. What should be used to remove this warning?

content.value:
- Use Index as the key

- Use Math.random().toString() as the key

options.text: a
b
Both a and b are correct
Both a and b are incorrect

questions.explanation: Both options remove the React unique key warning — React only requires a key prop to be present. Using the array **index** as a key is acceptable for static, non-reordered lists. Using `Math.random()` also removes the warning by supplying a key, but it is an anti-pattern: it generates a new key on every render, causing React to unmount and remount every list item, destroying component state and hurting performance. The question asks what _removes the warning_, not what is best practice — so both are technically correct.

questions.prompt: Alex is working on a project where she needs to implement a new feature requiring dynamic component loading. She plans to use React CLI for setting up the project and ensuring the feature integrates seamlessly. Considering her goal to optimize component handling and building times, which React CLI feature should Alex use to improve performance and manage components effectively?

options.text: Use the react-scripts to run and build components
Utilize create-react-app for efficient component management
Leverage custom React CLI script for specific component needs
Implement React CLI commands for module bundling and optimization.

These techniques allow components to be loaded on demand, reducing initial bundle size and improving build and runtime performance.

questions.title: What will be the possible output for the below program?
questions.prompt: What will be the possible output for the below program?

options.text: It will return an error.

It will return the values in data.
It will return a null value.

questions.explanation: React components must return JSX (or `null`), not plain JavaScript objects. Returning a plain object causes a runtime error: _"Objects are not valid as a React child."_ To render the data, you would need to map it into JSX elements.

questions.title: Which JSX will return by following the App Component?
questions.prompt: Which JSX will return by following the App Component?

options.text: Hello World!
World! Hello
Nothing will return
Error

questions.explanation: A React component can only return a single root element. Returning two adjacent `<div>` elements without a wrapper causes a compile-time error: _"Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped in an enclosing tag."_ The fix is to wrap them in a fragment `<>...</>` or a container element.

questions.prompt: Suppose you are working on an e-commerce website. You must create a production package. Which command will you use?

questions.title: A developer renders a list without a `key` prop. What is the primary risk?
questions.prompt: A developer renders a list without a `key` prop. What is the primary risk?

content.value:

    • );

options.text: The browser will throw a SyntaxError
React will silently skip items during updates
React cannot efficiently reconcile list items and may produce incorrect UI on re-renders

questions.title: A developer sees stale data after a state update. What is wrong with the following code?
questions.prompt: A developer sees stale data after a state update. What is wrong with the following code?

options.text: `useState` does not allow two updates in one function
Both calls read the same `count` snapshot, so `count` only increases by 1
The second `setCount` resets the state to 0
This pattern throws a React error

questions.explanation: State updates in React are batched. Both calls close over the same `count` value. Use the functional updater `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` to guarantee sequential increments.

questions.title: A developer passes a new object literal as a prop on every render. What is the consequence?
questions.prompt: A developer passes a new object literal as a prop on every render. What is the consequence?

content.value: <UserCard style={{ color: "blue" }} />

options.text: No consequence - React compares object values
React skips rendering because the reference is the same
`UserCard` will always re-render even if wrapped in `React.memo`, because the object reference changes
Passing objects as props is not allowed in React

questions.explanation: `React.memo` uses shallow comparison. A new object literal `{}` creates a new reference on every render, defeating memoization. Hoist the object outside the component or use `useMemo`.

questions.title: What does the following JSX compile to?
questions.prompt: What does the following JSX compile to?

options.text: `document.createElement("button")`
`React.createElement("button", { className: "btn", onClick: handleClick }, "Submit")`
`React.createComponent("button", ...)`
HTML string interpolation

questions.explanation: JSX is syntactic sugar. Babel (or the React transform) compiles JSX into `React.createElement(type, props, ...children)` calls that produce React element descriptor objects.

questions.title: A developer wraps several components with `withAuth(Component)` to enforce authentication. What React pattern does `withAuth` represent?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps several components with `withAuth(Component)` to enforce authentication. What React pattern does `withAuth` represent?

options.text: Render Props
Compound Components
Higher-Order Component (HOC)
Observer Pattern

questions.explanation: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function with the signature `(WrappedComponent) => EnhancedComponent`. It adds cross-cutting concerns (auth guards, logging, theming) without modifying the original component. In modern React, custom hooks have largely replaced HOCs for logic reuse, but HOCs remain common in legacy codebases and libraries.

questions.title: A developer needs to render a modal dialog outside the parent DOM node to avoid `overflow: hidden` and z-index stacking issues. Which React API solves this?
questions.prompt: A developer needs to render a modal dialog outside the parent DOM node to avoid `overflow: hidden` and z-index stacking issues. Which React API solves this?

options.text: `React.createContext`
`React.createPortal`
`React.lazy`
`React.forwardRef`

questions.explanation: `ReactDOM.createPortal(children, domNode)` renders children into any DOM node outside the component\'s parent hierarchy. Despite the separate DOM placement, React event bubbling still follows the React component tree — making portals ideal for modals, tooltips, and dropdown menus that must escape CSS overflow or z-index constraints.

questions.title: A developer has a component with no state, receiving only primitive props. Which optimization avoids re-rendering it when its parent re-renders with the same props?
questions.prompt: A developer has a component with no state, receiving only primitive props. Which optimization avoids re-rendering it when its parent re-renders with the same props?

options.text: Wrap it in `React.lazy()`
Extend `React.PureComponent` (class) or wrap with `React.memo` (function)
Move all logic into `useEffect`
Use `ReactDOM.createPortal`

questions.explanation: `React.PureComponent` performs a shallow comparison of props and state for class components. `React.memo` does the same for function components. Both prevent re-renders when props are shallowly unchanged — a lightweight optimization for "leaf" display components that receive only primitives or stable references.

questions.title: Suppose you are working on the use registration screen. You must call an input blur event from any other press event. Which React hook will you use?
questions.prompt: Suppose you are working on the use registration screen. You must call an input blur event from any other press event. Which React hook will you use?

options.text: useMemo
useReducer
useContext
useRef

questions.explanation: `useRef` gives you a direct reference to the underlying DOM element. By attaching the ref to the input (`<input ref={inputRef} />`), you can imperatively call `inputRef.current.blur()` from any other event handler to programmatically trigger the blur event.

questions.title: You are working on a food delivery web application. On the restaurant selection, you want to get elements from its stable unique ID. Which React hook will you use?
questions.prompt: You are working on a food delivery web application. On the restaurant selection, you want to get elements from its stable unique ID. Which React hook will you use?

options.text: useRef
useState
useId
useContext

questions.explanation: `useId` is a React hook that generates a stable, unique ID that is consistent between server and client renders. It is ideal for associating form elements with labels or any scenario requiring a guaranteed unique identifier per component instance.

questions.title: A developer wants to run a side effect only when `userId` changes. Which implementation is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer wants to run a side effect only when `userId` changes. Which implementation is correct?

options.text: Option A - runs on every render
Option B - runs once on mount

questions.explanation: Option C correctly lists `userId` as the only dependency. Option D is also valid if `fetchUser` is unstable, but Option C is the minimal correct answer for this scenario.

questions.title: A developer wraps an event handler with `useCallback` but still sees child re-renders. What is the likely cause?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps an event handler with `useCallback` but still sees child re-renders. What is the likely cause?

options.text: `useCallback` never prevents re-renders
`count` is in the dependency array, so `handleClick` is recreated every time `count` changes, causing the child to re-render
The child component must also use `useCallback`
`useCallback` requires a second argument of `true`

questions.explanation: Because `count` is a dependency, the callback is recreated on each count change, producing a new reference. Use `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` and remove `count` from the dependency array to keep a stable reference.

questions.title: What does `useMemo` return?
questions.prompt: What does `useMemo` return?

options.text: A memoized function
A memoized value - the sorted array, recomputed only when `items` changes
A ref to the previous render\'s sorted array
A state setter for the sorted list

questions.explanation: `useMemo` caches the result of the computation and only recomputes when a listed dependency changes. This avoids an expensive sort on every render.

questions.title: A developer uses `useRef` to hold a mutable value. What is true about this pattern?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `useRef` to hold a mutable value. What is true about this pattern?

options.text: Changing `timerRef.current` triggers a re-render
`timerRef.current` is reset to `null` on every render
Mutating `timerRef.current` does not cause a re-render and persists across renders
`useRef` can only hold DOM element references

questions.explanation: `useRef` returns a mutable container whose `.current` property survives re-renders without triggering them - ideal for storing timers, previous values, or DOM nodes.

questions.title: A developer uses the `useReducer` hook. When should it be preferred over `useState`?
questions.prompt: A developer uses the `useReducer` hook. When should it be preferred over `useState`?

content.value: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

options.text: When the state is a single boolean
When multiple sub-values depend on each other or next state depends on previous state in complex ways
Only when integrating with Redux
`useReducer` is deprecated in React 18+

questions.explanation: `useReducer` centralizes complex state transitions into a pure reducer function, making state logic easier to test and reason about compared to multiple independent `useState` calls.

questions.title: What makes `useWindowWidth` a valid custom hook?
questions.prompt: What makes `useWindowWidth` a valid custom hook?

options.text: The function accesses a browser API (`window`)
The function name starts with `use` and calls built-in React hooks internally, following the Rules of Hooks
The function returns exactly one value
The function must be exported from a dedicated file

questions.explanation: Custom hooks are plain JavaScript functions whose name begins with `use`. The `use` prefix signals to React\'s linter (eslint-plugin-react-hooks) that the function must follow the Rules of Hooks. They allow stateful logic to be shared across components without changing the component hierarchy or introducing HOC/render-prop complexity.

questions.title: A developer violates the Rules of Hooks. What is wrong with the following code?
questions.prompt: A developer violates the Rules of Hooks. What is wrong with the following code?

options.text: `useState` cannot be used in functional components
Hooks must not be called conditionally — the order of hook calls must be identical on every render
The `if` block should be replaced with `useEffect`
`isAdmin` must be listed in a dependency array

questions.explanation: React tracks each hook\'s state by its call order. Placing a hook inside an `if` block means it may or may not execute depending on the condition, corrupting React\'s internal state tracking. The fix is to call the hook unconditionally and use the condition inside it: `const [role, setRole] = useState(isAdmin ? "admin" : "")`.

questions.title: A developer calls `useContext(ThemeContext)` inside a component. When does the component re-render?
questions.prompt: A developer calls `useContext(ThemeContext)` inside a component. When does the component re-render?

options.text: Every time any state changes anywhere in the application
Only when the component\'s own state changes
Whenever the `value` prop of the nearest `ThemeContext.Provider` above it changes
`useContext` never causes a re-render

questions.explanation: `useContext` subscribes the component to context updates. React re-renders the consumer whenever the `value` reference on the matching Provider changes. To prevent unnecessary re-renders, memoize the context value with `useMemo` so it only changes when the underlying data changes.

questions.title: What does the cleanup function returned from `useEffect` do?
questions.prompt: What does the cleanup function returned from `useEffect` do?

options.text: It runs before the component mounts for the first time
It runs after every re-render before the next effect executes, and on unmount
It runs only when the component unmounts
It cancels the `subscribe` call before it resolves

questions.explanation: React calls the cleanup function before re-running the effect due to a dependency change, and also when the component unmounts. This prevents stale subscriptions and memory leaks.

questions.title: A class component uses `componentDidUpdate`. What is its hooks-based equivalent?
questions.prompt: A class component uses `componentDidUpdate`. What is its hooks-based equivalent?

options.text: `useEffect(() => { fetchData(id); }, [])`
`useEffect(() => { fetchData(id); }, [id])`
`useLayoutEffect(() => { fetchData(id); })`
`useMemo(() => fetchData(id), [id])`

questions.explanation: Listing `id` in the dependency array replicates the `prevProps.id !== this.props.id` guard - the effect only re-runs when `id` changes.

questions.title: A developer notices a layout flash when reading a DOM node\'s size. Which hook should replace `useEffect`?
questions.prompt: A developer notices a layout flash when reading a DOM node\'s size. Which hook should replace `useEffect`?

options.text: `useRef`
`useMemo`
`useLayoutEffect`
`useTransition`

questions.explanation: `useLayoutEffect` fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but before the browser paints, allowing DOM measurements and mutations without a visible flash.

questions.title: What is the `useEffect` equivalent of `componentDidMount` in a class component?
questions.prompt: What is the `useEffect` equivalent of `componentDidMount` in a class component?

options.text: Option A — runs after every render
Option B — runs once after the initial render only
Option C — runs after mount and when `fetchInitialData` changes
There is no hooks equivalent of `componentDidMount`

questions.explanation: `useEffect` with an empty dependency array `[]` runs exactly once after the component\'s first render, mirroring `componentDidMount`. Option A runs after every render (no equivalent lifecycle); Option C also re-runs if `fetchInitialData` reference changes, which is not the same as `componentDidMount`.

questions.title: A developer fetches data inside `useEffect` and updates state, but gets a warning: _"Can\'t perform a React state update on an unmounted component."_ What is the correct fix?
questions.prompt: A developer fetches data inside `useEffect` and updates state, but gets a warning: _"Can\'t perform a React state update on an unmounted component."_ What is the correct fix?

Use a cleanup function with an `isMounted` flag or `AbortController` to cancel the update after unmount
Wrap `setUser` in a `try/catch` block
Replace `useEffect` with `useLayoutEffect`

questions.title: A class component uses `shouldComponentUpdate` to skip re-renders. What is the functional component equivalent?
questions.prompt: A class component uses `shouldComponentUpdate` to skip re-renders. What is the functional component equivalent?

options.text: `useEffect` with a comparison inside
`React.memo` with a custom comparator function as the second argument
`useMemo` wrapping the entire JSX return
`useCallback` on the render function

questions.title: React 19 introduces the `use()` hook. What does the following code do?
questions.prompt: React 19 introduces the `use()` hook. What does the following code do?

options.text: `use()` converts a class component to a function component
`use()` reads a Promise or Context value, suspending the component until the Promise resolves
`use()` replaces `useEffect` for data fetching
`use()` is equivalent to `await` inside a component

questions.explanation: `use()` is a new React 19 hook that can be called conditionally (unlike other hooks). It integrates with Suspense - the component suspends while the Promise is pending and resumes with the resolved value.

questions.title: A developer uses the React 19 `useFormStatus` hook. What data does it expose?
questions.prompt: A developer uses the React 19 `useFormStatus` hook. What data does it expose?

options.text: Validation errors for the parent form fields
The submission state of the nearest parent `<form>`, including whether a submission is pending
The HTTP response status code of the form\'s action
The names and values of all form fields

questions.explanation: `useFormStatus` (react-dom) gives child components access to the form\'s submission state. `pending` is `true` while the form action is executing, enabling progressive-enhancement UX patterns.

questions.title: What is the purpose of `useOptimistic` in React 19?
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `useOptimistic` in React 19?

options.text: To batch multiple state updates together
To immediately show an optimistic UI update while an async action is in flight, then reconcile with the real result
To cache server responses in memory
To preload assets before the component mounts

questions.explanation: `useOptimistic` lets you speculatively update the UI before the server confirms the action. Once the action settles, React replaces the optimistic state with the real server state.

questions.title: A developer migrates a form to use React 19 Server Actions. Which statement is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer migrates a form to use React 19 Server Actions. Which statement is correct?

options.text: `"use server"` marks the whole file as a server-only module
The `action` prop on `<form>` only accepts a URL string
The async function runs on the server; passing it to `action` enables progressive enhancement without a client-side JS handler
Server Actions require Redux to manage resulting state

questions.explanation: React 19 Server Actions allow async functions marked `"use server"` to be passed directly to `<form action>`. The form works even without JavaScript, and React manages serialization automatically.

questions.title: In React 19, what changed about `ref` handling for function components?
questions.prompt: In React 19, what changed about `ref` handling for function components?

options.text: `ref` is no longer supported on function components
Function components can now accept `ref` as a regular prop without `forwardRef`
`ref` must be passed as `innerRef` in React 19
`useRef` was replaced by `createRef` in function components

questions.explanation: React 19 deprecates `forwardRef`. Function components can receive `ref` directly in their props, simplifying ref forwarding patterns significantly.

questions.title: A developer dispatches an action but the UI does not update. What is the most likely bug?
questions.prompt: A developer dispatches an action but the UI does not update. What is the most likely bug?

options.text: `push` is not a valid JavaScript array method
The reducer mutates state directly and returns the same reference - React-Redux cannot detect the change
Actions must be strings, not objects
The component needs to call `forceUpdate()`

questions.explanation: Redux reducers must be pure functions that return a new state object. Mutating and returning the same reference means React-Redux\'s shallow equality check sees no change and skips re-rendering. Return `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] }` instead.

questions.title: What is the role of middleware such as `redux-thunk`?
questions.prompt: What is the role of middleware such as `redux-thunk`?

options.text: It replaces the Redux store entirely for async operations
It allows action creators to return functions (thunks) instead of plain objects, enabling async logic
It validates action types at runtime
It replaces `combineReducers` for large applications

questions.explanation: Plain Redux only handles synchronous plain-object actions. `redux-thunk` intercepts function actions and calls them with `dispatch` and `getState`, enabling async workflows.

questions.title: A developer uses `useSelector` and notices unnecessary re-renders. What is the cause?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `useSelector` and notices unnecessary re-renders. What is the cause?

options.text: `useSelector` does not support object return values
A new object literal is returned on every call, so the selector\'s reference always changes, triggering a re-render
Both `user` and `posts` need separate stores
`useSelector` is not allowed inside function components

questions.explanation: `useSelector` uses reference equality by default. Returning a new object `{}` each time always fails the equality check. Use separate `useSelector` calls, `shallowEqual` as the second argument, or `createSelector` from Reselect.

questions.title: What is the purpose of `combineReducers`?
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `combineReducers`?

options.text: It merges multiple Redux stores into one
It splits a single large reducer into slice functions, each managing its own part of the state tree
It enables lazy loading of reducers
It prevents reducers from receiving unknown actions

questions.explanation: `combineReducers` delegates different parts of the state to separate reducer functions. Each reducer only receives and manages its own slice of the state (`state.auth`, `state.cart`, etc.).

questions.title: A developer uses `createSlice`. What does `createSlice` automatically generate?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `createSlice`. What does `createSlice` automatically generate?

options.text: Only the reducer function
The reducer and corresponding action creators (`counterSlice.actions`)
The Redux store and DevTools configuration
Async thunks for each reducer

questions.explanation: `createSlice` uses Immer under the hood (enabling safe mutation syntax) and auto-generates action creators whose `type` matches `"sliceName/reducerName"` - e.g., `"counter/increment"`.

questions.title: A developer uses `createAsyncThunk`. What lifecycle actions does it dispatch?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `createAsyncThunk`. What lifecycle actions does it dispatch?

options.text: Only `posts/fetchAll`
`posts/fetchAll/pending`, `posts/fetchAll/fulfilled`, `posts/fetchAll/rejected`
`REQUEST`, `SUCCESS`, `FAILURE`
`START`, `DONE`, `ERROR`

questions.explanation: `createAsyncThunk` automatically dispatches `pending` before the Promise starts, `fulfilled` on resolution, and `rejected` on rejection - matching the FSA lifecycle convention.

questions.title: A developer uses RTK Query\'s `createApi`. What does the following `useGetUserQuery` hook return?
questions.prompt: A developer uses RTK Query\'s `createApi`. What does the following `useGetUserQuery` hook return?

options.text: A Promise that must be awaited manually
An object with `data`, loading/error state, and refetch helpers - auto-fetching when `userId` changes
Only the raw fetch response object
A Redux action creator

questions.explanation: RTK Query auto-generates hooks that manage fetching, caching, and re-fetching. The hook re-fetches whenever `userId` changes and handles deduplication and cache invalidation automatically.

questions.title: A developer forgets to add the RTK Query API reducer to the store. What happens?
questions.prompt: A developer forgets to add the RTK Query API reducer to the store. What happens?

options.text: RTK Query works fine - the middleware handles everything
RTK Query cannot store its cache; queries will always refetch and cache features will not work
The app crashes immediately on startup
Only mutations will fail; queries work without the reducer

questions.explanation: RTK Query stores its normalized cache in the Redux state tree under `api.reducerPath`. Without the reducer, there is nowhere to persist data and the cache/invalidation system will not function.

questions.title: A developer wants to respond to `fetchPosts` (a `createAsyncThunk`) inside a `createSlice`. Where should the thunk lifecycle actions be handled?
questions.prompt: A developer wants to respond to `fetchPosts` (a `createAsyncThunk`) inside a `createSlice`. Where should the thunk lifecycle actions be handled?

options.text: Inside the `reducers` field with matching action type strings
Inside `extraReducers` using the builder callback: `builder.addCase(fetchPosts.fulfilled, ...)`
In a separate `createReducer` call outside the slice
Directly inside the component with `useDispatch` and a `useEffect`

questions.explanation: `extraReducers` is the correct location to handle actions that were generated outside the slice — such as thunk lifecycle actions from `createAsyncThunk`. The builder API provides type-safe methods (`addCase`, `addMatcher`, `addDefaultCase`) to react to `pending`, `fulfilled`, and `rejected` states.

questions.title: A developer uses `createSelector` from Redux Toolkit (Reselect). What problem does it solve?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `createSelector` from Redux Toolkit (Reselect). What problem does it solve?

options.text: It replaces `useSelector` for all state access
It memoizes derived data — the result function re-runs only when the input selectors return new values, preventing unnecessary recomputation and re-renders
It validates the shape of the Redux state tree
It auto-generates action creators for each selector

questions.explanation: Without memoization, a selector computing derived data (filtered lists, sorted arrays, aggregates) runs on every render. `createSelector` caches the last result and skips recomputation when its input selectors return the same references, improving both CPU usage and render performance when used with `useSelector`.

questions.title: Alex, an experienced engineer, is optimizing an application\'s event-driven architecture to handle high-frequency events more efficiently. She needs a strategy that will minimize performance bottlenecks and ensure scalability. Which approach should Alex adopt to effectively manage and optimize event handling in the application?
questions.prompt: Alex, an experienced engineer, is optimizing an application\'s event-driven architecture to handle high-frequency events more efficiently. She needs a strategy that will minimize performance bottlenecks and ensure scalability. Which approach should Alex adopt to effectively manage and optimize event handling in the application?

options.text: Implementing a Debounce function to limit the rate at which events are processed.
Using a Global Event Bus to broadcast events across multiple components.
Applying the Observer pattern to allow components to state changes efficiently.
Integrating a Redux middleware to handle asynchronous events and manage side effects.

questions.explanation: Debouncing limits how often a high-frequency event handler fires by delaying execution until a burst of events has stopped. This directly reduces performance bottlenecks for events like scroll, resize, or keypress. A Global Event Bus adds coupling, the Observer pattern addresses subscriptions not rate-limiting, and Redux middleware handles async side effects rather than event frequency.

questions.title: Suppose you are working on an inventory management portal. When your product list loads, you don\'t have any control over its state but you want to give high priority to UI updates. Which React feature will help you?
questions.prompt: Suppose you are working on an inventory management portal. When your product list loads, you don\'t have any control over its state but you want to give high priority to UI updates. Which React feature will help you?

options.text: useTransition
useEffect
useMemo
useDeferredValue

questions.explanation: `useDeferredValue` is the right choice when you do not control the state (e.g., it comes from a prop or an external source). It creates a deferred copy of the value so React can prioritize urgent UI updates and render the deferred value when the browser is idle. `useTransition` is similar but requires you to own the state update.

questions.title: A parent re-renders frequently. A child component receives the same props every time. How do you prevent the child from re-rendering?
questions.prompt: A parent re-renders frequently. A child component receives the same props every time. How do you prevent the child from re-rendering?

options.text: Wrap `Child` in `React.lazy()`
Wrap `Child` in `React.memo()` - it skips re-rendering if props did not shallowly change
Use `useEffect` inside `Child` to guard rendering
Move `Child` into the parent\'s render method

questions.explanation: `React.memo` is a higher-order component that memoizes the rendered output. If the next props shallowly equal the previous props, React reuses the last render and skips the child\'s reconciliation.

questions.title: A developer profiles the app and sees a slow computation running on every render. Which hook should they apply?
questions.prompt: A developer profiles the app and sees a slow computation running on every render. Which hook should they apply?

options.text: `useEffect` - run the computation as a side effect
`useCallback` - memoize the reduce function
`useMemo` - cache the computed `total` and recompute only when `transactions` changes
`useRef` - store the total in a ref

questions.explanation: `useMemo(() => transactions.reduce(...), [transactions])` ensures the expensive reduction only runs when `transactions` changes, not on every render.

questions.title: A developer uses `useTransition`. What does `isPending` indicate?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `useTransition`. What does `isPending` indicate?

options.text: The network request is in-flight
React is still processing the low-priority transition update
The component is suspended in a Suspense boundary
The input field has unsaved changes

questions.explanation: `useTransition` marks an update as non-urgent. `isPending` is `true` while React is rendering the deferred update, allowing you to show a loading indicator without blocking the input.

questions.title: Suppose you have a three-level component hierarchy and must pass a value from the top component to the leaf component, but using props shall take extra code. How can you achieve this without using props?
questions.prompt: Suppose you have a three-level component hierarchy and must pass a value from the top component to the leaf component, but using props shall take extra code. How can you achieve this without using props?

options.text: Use the Context API
Use the Event Bus
Use a common file for this type of values
Use the Custom component

questions.explanation: The React Context API is designed exactly for this scenario — passing data through a component tree without having to thread props through every intermediate level (prop drilling). Create a context with `React.createContext`, wrap the tree in a `Provider`, and any descendant can consume the value with `useContext`.

questions.title: A developer wraps the app in a `ThemeContext.Provider`. A deeply nested component reads the theme. What happens when the theme value changes?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps the app in a `ThemeContext.Provider`. A deeply nested component reads the theme. What happens when the theme value changes?

content.value:
<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>
  <App />
</ThemeContext.Provider>

options.text: Only the direct children of `Provider` re-render
All components that consume the context via `useContext(ThemeContext)` re-render
The entire component tree re-renders regardless of context consumption
Context changes do not trigger re-renders; components must call `forceUpdate`

questions.explanation: React re-renders every component that called `useContext(ThemeContext)` whenever the `value` reference changes. Components that do not consume the context are not affected.

questions.title: A developer notices that changing an unrelated state in the Provider\'s parent causes all consumers to re-render. What is the fix?
questions.prompt: A developer notices that changing an unrelated state in the Provider\'s parent causes all consumers to re-render. What is the fix?

options.text: Move context into Redux
Use `useMemo` to stabilize the `theme` object reference
Split the context into two providers
Switch to a class component

questions.explanation: A new `theme` object is created on every render, causing all consumers to re-render. `const theme = useMemo(() => ({ color: "blue" }), [])` produces a stable reference and prevents unnecessary consumer updates.

questions.title: Alex, a software engineer, encounters an unhandled promise rejection error in an application. He observes that while the app displays an error message, the error details are not logged effectively for debugging. How can Alex ensure comprehensive error logging for unhandled promise rejections?
questions.prompt: Alex, a software engineer, encounters an unhandled promise rejection error in an application. He observes that while the app displays an error message, the error details are not logged effectively for debugging. How can Alex ensure comprehensive error logging for unhandled promise rejections?

options.text: Use window.addEventListener to listen for unhandled promise rejections and log them.
Configure the app to catch error in async functions using try-catch blocks.
Implement a global error boundary component to handle and log all errors
Integrate a logging library that automatically captures unhandled promises rejections.

questions.explanation: `window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', handler)` is the standard browser API for globally capturing unhandled promise rejections. The event object provides the rejected `reason`, enabling comprehensive logging. Error Boundaries do not catch async/promise errors, and `try-catch` only works when applied locally around each async call.

questions.title: A developer wraps a component tree in an Error Boundary. Which types of errors does it catch?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps a component tree in an Error Boundary. Which types of errors does it catch?

options.text: All JavaScript errors anywhere in the application
Errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of child components
Errors thrown inside event handlers
Network errors from `fetch` calls

questions.explanation: Error Boundaries catch errors during React\'s render phase and lifecycle methods. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers (use `try/catch` there), async code, or server-side rendering.

questions.title: What is the difference between `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`?

options.text: They are identical; either can be used
`getDerivedStateFromError` is used to render a fallback UI (render phase); `componentDidCatch` is used to log error information (commit phase)
`componentDidCatch` renders the fallback; `getDerivedStateFromError` only logs
`getDerivedStateFromError` replaces `componentDidCatch` in React 18+

questions.explanation: `getDerivedStateFromError` runs during rendering so it can update state to show a fallback. `componentDidCatch` runs after the tree has re-rendered and is the right place to call error reporting services.

questions.title: You are working on a real-time stock market web application. As your dashboard code is too lengthy, it takes excess time to load. How will you resolve this issue?
questions.prompt: You are working on a real-time stock market web application. As your dashboard code is too lengthy, it takes excess time to load. How will you resolve this issue?

options.text: Remove a few features from the page
Split the code into small modules and import it as per the requirements.
Remove a few data load requests and make it light
Limit data that increases the load on the dashboard.

questions.explanation: Code splitting with `React.lazy()` and dynamic `import()` allows the dashboard to load only the code needed for the initial view, deferring heavier modules until they are required. This reduces the initial bundle size and improves load time without removing features or limiting data.

questions.title: Alex, a software developer, is working on an application where she needs to implement a seamless transition between pages. She is considering using the Transition API to enhance the user experience. Which approach should Alex take to achieve smooth transitions in her application?
questions.prompt: Alex, a software developer, is working on an application where she needs to implement a seamless transition between pages. She is considering using the Transition API to enhance the user experience. Which approach should Alex take to achieve smooth transitions in her application?

options.text: Use the Transition API\'s startTransition function to update the state that triggers transitions.
Apply the ReactDom.createRoot method to manage the rendering of transition states.
Utilize React.StrictMode to detect potential issues during transitions.
Implement React.lazy for dynamic imports to handle page transitions.

questions.explanation: `startTransition` (from `useTransition` or `React.startTransition`) marks a state update as a non-urgent transition, allowing React to keep the current UI responsive while preparing the new page in the background. This is the correct way to achieve smooth page-to-page transitions with the Transition API.

questions.title: Alex, a software developer, is working on an application where she is utilizing Suspense for handling data fetching. Despite configuring Suspense she observes that her component does not render immediately when waiting for data. She is puzzled about the potential reasons behind this delay in rendering. What could be the reason for this behavior?
questions.prompt: Alex, a software developer, is working on an application where she is utilizing Suspense for handling data fetching. Despite configuring Suspense she observes that her component does not render immediately when waiting for data. She is puzzled about the potential reasons behind this delay in rendering. What could be the reason for this behavior?

options.text: The delay in rendering might be due to network latency or slow data fetching, rather than an issue with how Suspense is used or configured in the application.
Alex\'s component could be using an outdated version that does not support the latest features required for Suspense to handle data fetching and rendering efficiently, resulting in the delay.

The Suspense component configuration might be incorrect or incomplete. If Suspense is not properly set up, it could lead to unexpected delays in rendering the component and handling asynchronous operations.

Alex might not have wrapped her component properly with a Suspense component. This is crucial as Suspense manages asynchronous data fetching and ensures that the fallback UI is shown until the data is fully loaded and the component is ready to render.

questions.explanation: Suspense requires components that perform asynchronous data fetching to be wrapped inside a `<Suspense>` boundary with a `fallback` prop. Without proper wrapping, the component will not know to show a fallback UI while data loads, resulting in unexpected rendering behavior.

questions.title: A developer lazy-loads a component. Why is `Suspense` required?
questions.prompt: A developer lazy-loads a component. Why is `Suspense` required?

options.text: `Suspense` fetches the chunk from the network
While the `Chart` chunk is downloading, the component suspends; `Suspense` provides the fallback UI during that pause
`Suspense` caches the chunk so it is only downloaded once
Without `Suspense`, `React.lazy` defaults to eager loading

questions.explanation: `React.lazy` throws a Promise while the module is loading. A `Suspense` boundary catches that Promise and renders its `fallback` prop until the Promise resolves and the component is ready.

questions.title: A developer code-splits by route. Which approach is correct for React Router v6?
questions.prompt: A developer code-splits by route. Which approach is correct for React Router v6?

options.text: Option A is correct
Option B is correct
Both are equivalent
Neither is valid - React Router handles code splitting automatically

questions.explanation: Dynamic `import()` must be wrapped in `React.lazy()` and the resulting component must be rendered inside a `Suspense` boundary. Option B creates a Promise, not a React component.

questions.title: A developer builds a controlled input. What is missing?
questions.prompt: A developer builds a controlled input. What is missing?

options.text: The `defaultValue` attribute
An `onChange` handler - without it the input is read-only and cannot be updated
A `ref` to read the input value
`name` attribute for the controlled input

questions.explanation: In a controlled component, React drives the input value via the `value` prop. Without `onChange` calling `setQuery`, user keystrokes are ignored and the input appears frozen.

questions.title: A developer uses React Hook Form. What advantage does it have over fully controlled forms?
questions.prompt: A developer uses React Hook Form. What advantage does it have over fully controlled forms?

options.text: It eliminates the need for any validation logic
It uses uncontrolled inputs with refs by default, reducing re-renders on every keystroke
It replaces the native HTML `<form>` element
It is only useful for very large forms

questions.explanation: React Hook Form avoids re-rendering on each keystroke by managing values through DOM refs instead of React state, significantly improving performance for complex forms.

questions.title: A developer wants to manage multiple form inputs with a single state object. Which pattern is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer wants to manage multiple form inputs with a single state object. Which pattern is correct?

options.text: Option A — uses computed property names to update only the changed field immutably
Option B — directly mutates the state object then sets it
Both are equivalent
Neither is valid; each input requires its own `useState`

questions.explanation: `[e.target.name]` is a computed property key that dynamically targets the right field. The spread `...form` ensures the rest of the state is preserved immutably. Option B mutates the existing state object directly and passes the same reference, so React may not detect the change and re-render.

questions.title: What is the key difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled component?
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled component?

options.text: Controlled components are faster because they skip React reconciliation
In a controlled component, React owns the value via state; in an uncontrolled component, the DOM owns the value and it is read via a ref
Uncontrolled components do not support `onChange` events
`defaultValue` is only valid in controlled components

questions.explanation: Controlled components keep the input value in React state, making it the single source of truth. Uncontrolled components let the DOM manage the value — you read it imperatively via `ref.current.value` (e.g., on submit). Controlled inputs are preferred when you need immediate validation or conditional rendering based on input value.

questions.title: A developer renders a `<select>` dropdown as a controlled component. What is wrong with the following code?
questions.prompt: A developer renders a `<select>` dropdown as a controlled component. What is wrong with the following code?

options.text: `<select>` cannot be a controlled component in React
The `value` prop is missing on `<select>` and there is no `onChange` handler — the selection is uncontrolled
Each `<option>` needs its own `onChange` handler
`useState` cannot be used with `<select>` elements

questions.explanation: In React, a controlled `<select>` requires `value={color}` on the element and `onChange={e => setColor(e.target.value)}` to keep the state in sync with the selected option — the same pattern as a controlled `<input>`. Without `value`, the browser manages the selection independently of React state.

questions.title: A developer writes the following test. What does `jest.fn()` return?
questions.prompt: A developer writes the following test. What does `jest.fn()` return?

options.text: `["hello", "world"]`
`[["hello"], ["world"]]` - an array of arrays, one per call
`{ args: ["hello", "world"] }`
The number of times the function was called

questions.explanation: `jest.fn()` creates a mock function. `mock.calls` is an array where each element is an array of arguments from a single invocation. Useful for asserting what arguments the mock received.

questions.title: A developer tests an async function. Why does this test always pass even when it should fail?
questions.prompt: A developer tests an async function. Why does this test always pass even when it should fail?

options.text: The assertion is inside a `.then()` and Jest does not know to wait for it
`fetchUser` is synchronous
`.then()` callbacks run before the test ends
`expect` is not supported inside `.then()`

questions.explanation: Jest completes the test when the synchronous function returns. The `.then()` callback runs asynchronously after Jest has already marked the test as passed. Use `async/await` or return the Promise to fix this.

questions.title: What is a Jest snapshot test doing in the following scenario?
questions.prompt: What is a Jest snapshot test doing in the following scenario?

options.text: It takes a screenshot of the rendered component
On first run it serializes the component output to a `.snap` file; subsequent runs compare output against that saved snapshot
It validates the component against a JSON schema
It renders the component inside a headless browser

questions.explanation: Snapshot tests serialize the rendered output. If the output changes unexpectedly, the test fails. Run `jest --updateSnapshot` to intentionally update the saved snapshot after a deliberate change.

questions.title: A developer needs to mock a module dependency in Jest. Which approach is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer needs to mock a module dependency in Jest. Which approach is correct?

options.text: `jest.mock` must be called after the `import` statement
`jest.mock("./api")` auto-mocks the module; calling `mockResolvedValue` sets the resolved value for that test
`mockResolvedValue` only works for `jest.spyOn`, not `jest.mock`
The mock file must be placed in a `__mocks__` folder

questions.explanation: `jest.mock` is hoisted before imports by Babel, replacing all exports with `jest.fn()`. `mockResolvedValue` configures the mock to resolve with the given value, simulating a successful async API call.

questions.title: A developer uses `beforeEach` and `afterEach`. What is their purpose?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `beforeEach` and `afterEach`. What is their purpose?

options.text: They run once before and after the entire `describe` block
`beforeEach` runs before each individual test; `afterEach` runs after each individual test - ensuring test isolation
They are only needed when testing async code
They replace the `test()` setup and teardown lifecycle

questions.explanation: `beforeEach`/`afterEach` are test lifecycle hooks that set up and tear down state around each individual test, preventing state leakage between tests. Use `beforeAll`/`afterAll` for once-per-suite setup.

questions.title: A developer queries a button using `getByRole`. Why is this preferred over `getByTestId`?
questions.prompt: A developer queries a button using `getByRole`. Why is this preferred over `getByTestId`?

content.value: const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i });

options.text: `getByRole` is faster than `getByTestId`
`getByRole` queries the DOM the way assistive technologies do, making tests more accessible and resilient to implementation details
`getByTestId` is not supported in React Testing Library
`getByRole` does not require any HTML attributes

questions.explanation: The Testing Library philosophy is to test from a user\'s perspective. `getByRole` mirrors how screen readers navigate the DOM, and tests that break only when real user-visible behavior changes.

questions.title: A developer tests a form submission. What does `userEvent.click` do compared to `fireEvent.click`?
questions.prompt: A developer tests a form submission. What does `userEvent.click` do compared to `fireEvent.click`?

options.text: They are identical in behavior
`userEvent.click` simulates a full browser interaction (pointerdown, mousedown, mouseup, click) while `fireEvent.click` dispatches only the click event
`fireEvent.click` is async; `userEvent.click` is synchronous
`userEvent` is only available in Cypress, not React Testing Library

questions.explanation: `@testing-library/user-event` simulates realistic user interactions including all intermediate events, making tests closer to real browser behavior. `fireEvent` dispatches a single synthetic event.

questions.title: A developer needs to wait for an async update after an action. Which assertion is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer needs to wait for an async update after an action. Which assertion is correct?

options.text: `findByText` will throw immediately if "Alice" is not in the DOM
`findByText` is equivalent to `getByText` and does not wait
`findByText` returns a Promise that retries the query until the element appears or times out
`await` is not needed because React Testing Library is synchronous

questions.explanation: `findBy*` queries combine `waitFor` and `getBy*`. They poll the DOM at intervals until the element appears or the timeout (default 1000 ms) expires, making them ideal for testing async rendering.

questions.title: A developer needs to test that an element is NOT present in the DOM. Which approach is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer needs to test that an element is NOT present in the DOM. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Option A - `getByText` returns null when the element is absent
Option B - `queryByText` returns `null` when not found (does not throw); suitable for asserting absence
Both are equivalent
Neither is valid; use `findByText` with `not`

questions.explanation: `getBy*` throws an error when an element is not found. `queryBy*` returns `null` instead, which is the correct variant when you need to assert the element is absent.

questions.title: A Redux-connected component needs testing. What is the recommended setup?
questions.prompt: A Redux-connected component needs testing. What is the recommended setup?

options.text: Always mock the entire Redux store with `jest.mock("react-redux")`
Wrap the component in a real Redux `Provider` with a test store that has a known `preloadedState`
Use `useSelector` directly in test files instead of rendering the component
Testing Redux-connected components requires Enzyme

questions.explanation: Using a real store with `preloadedState` keeps tests realistic and avoids brittle mocks. Redux Toolkit\'s `configureStore` is lightweight enough to spin up per test. This is the pattern recommended by the Redux and RTL maintainers.

questions.title: Alex created a component, Rxjs.js, and imported an observable from the RxJS library, like this:
questions.prompt: Alex created a component, Rxjs.js, and imported an observable from the RxJS library, like this:

Use the Observable without adding the new keyword before it: const observable = Observable ((subscriber)=> {...})
Change the Observable name to something else to make it work
Change the file name to something else to make the RxJS work

questions.explanation: The code uses `import {Observables} from 'Rxjs'` which has two problems: the named import is misspelled as `Observables` (should be `Observable`), and the package name `'Rxjs'` should be lowercase `'rxjs'`. The correct import is `import { Observable } from 'rxjs'`. The `new` keyword is also required when constructing an Observable, so option B is incorrect.

questions.title: What is the purpose of `React.StrictMode`?
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `React.StrictMode`?

content.value:
<React.StrictMode>
  <App />
</React.StrictMode>

options.text: It enables server-side rendering for the wrapped components
It renders components twice in development to detect side effects, and warns about deprecated APIs
It prevents any mutations to props or state at runtime
It activates performance optimizations similar to production mode

questions.explanation: `React.StrictMode` is a development-only tool with no visible UI. It intentionally double-invokes render functions, state initializers, and `useEffect` cleanup/setup pairs to surface components with impure side effects. It also warns when deprecated lifecycle methods or APIs are used. It has no effect in production.

questions.title: A developer wraps siblings in `<React.Fragment>` instead of a `<div>`. What is the benefit?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps siblings in `<React.Fragment>` instead of a `<div>`. What is the benefit?

options.text: `React.Fragment` improves performance by skipping reconciliation
It groups elements without adding an extra DOM node, preserving valid HTML structure
It is required when returning more than two elements
`React.Fragment` enables CSS Grid layout for its children

questions.explanation: `<React.Fragment>` (or the shorthand `<>...</>`) allows a component to return multiple elements without a wrapper `<div>`. This is critical for cases like `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs inside a `<dl>`, or `<tr>`/`<td>` in a table, where an extra `<div>` would break valid HTML semantics. The fragment itself is not rendered to the DOM.

questions.title: A developer uses the `key` prop on a component outside of a list to reset its state. What does this achieve?
questions.prompt: A developer uses the `key` prop on a component outside of a list to reset its state. What does this achieve?

content.value: <ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />

options.text: It adds the component to an internal React registry
Changing `key` causes React to unmount the old component instance and mount a fresh one, fully resetting all internal state
The `key` prop only affects performance, not component identity
This is invalid — `key` may only be used on list items

questions.explanation: React uses `key` to identify component instances across renders. When `key` changes, React treats it as a completely different component — it unmounts the old tree and mounts a new one. This is a deliberate pattern to reset a component\'s state when switching context (e.g., navigating between user profiles) without lifting state up or adding `useEffect` reset logic.

questions.title: Which command scaffolds a new Next.js project with the latest version?
questions.prompt: Which command scaffolds a new Next.js project with the latest version?

options.text: `npx create-react-app --template next`
`npx create-next-app@latest`
`npm init next-app`
`npx next init`

questions.explanation: The official scaffold tool is `create-next-app`. Running `npx create-next-app@latest` interactively prompts for TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind CSS, the `src/` directory structure, and whether to use the App Router.

questions.title: In the Next.js Pages Router, a component exported from `pages/blog/index.js` maps to which URL path?
questions.prompt: In the Next.js Pages Router, a component exported from `pages/blog/index.js` maps to which URL path?

options.text: `/pages/blog`
`/blog/index`
`/blog`
`/blog/index.js`

questions.explanation: Next.js uses file-based routing. An `index.js` file maps to the root of its directory segment, so `pages/blog/index.js` resolves to `/blog`. This mirrors standard web server conventions for index files.

questions.title: Which Next.js built-in component should be used for client-side navigation to avoid a full page reload?
questions.prompt: Which Next.js built-in component should be used for client-side navigation to avoid a full page reload?

options.text: `<a href="/about">`
`<Router to="/about">`
`<Link href="/about">` from `next/link`
`<Navigate to="/about">`

questions.explanation: The `<Link>` component from `next/link` intercepts clicks and performs client-side route transitions using the browser History API. It also prefetches linked pages in the background in production, delivering near-instant navigation — unlike a plain `<a>` tag which triggers a full page reload.

questions.title: What advantage does `next/image` offer over a plain HTML `` tag?
questions.prompt: What advantage does `next/image` offer over a plain HTML `` tag?

options.text: Support for SVG animations
Automatic image optimization, lazy loading by default, and responsive `srcset` generation
Built-in CSS filter effects
Client-side image cropping and editing

questions.explanation: `next/image` passes images through Next.js\'s built-in optimization pipeline: it converts to modern formats (WebP/AVIF), resizes on demand, lazy-loads by default, and prevents cumulative layout shift (CLS) by requiring explicit `width` and `height` props. This significantly improves Core Web Vitals scores.

questions.title: What is the key difference between `getStaticProps` and `getServerSideProps` in the Next.js Pages Router?
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `getStaticProps` and `getServerSideProps` in the Next.js Pages Router?

options.text: Both run on the server and produce identical output
`getStaticProps` runs at build time (SSG); `getServerSideProps` runs on every incoming request (SSR)
`getStaticProps` is only for API routes
`getServerSideProps` permanently caches its result

questions.explanation: `getStaticProps` pre-renders pages at build time, producing static HTML that can be cached at a CDN edge — ideal for content that rarely changes. `getServerSideProps` generates fresh HTML per request, granting access to real-time data, request cookies, and headers, but at the cost of higher server latency.

questions.title: A developer needs a dynamic route for individual product pages at `/products/[id]`. Which file path in the Pages Router is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer needs a dynamic route for individual product pages at `/products/[id]`. Which file path in the Pages Router is correct?

options.text: `pages/products/:id.js`
`pages/products/{id}.js`
`pages/products/[id].js`
`pages/products/$id.js`

questions.explanation: Next.js uses square-bracket notation for dynamic route segments. `pages/products/[id].js` matches `/products/42`, `/products/abc`, etc. The dynamic value is accessible as `router.query.id` or via the `params` argument in `getStaticProps` / `getServerSideProps`.

questions.title: A developer creates `pages/api/orders.js`. What does this file expose?
questions.prompt: A developer creates `pages/api/orders.js`. What does this file expose?

options.text: A React page component rendered at `/api/orders`
A serverless API endpoint that handles HTTP requests at `/api/orders`
A static JSON file served at `/api/orders`
A WebSocket connection endpoint

questions.explanation: Files inside `pages/api/` are API routes that run exclusively on the server. They receive Node.js-style `req` and `res` objects, are never sent to the browser, and keep server-only logic (database queries, secret keys) completely isolated from the client bundle.

questions.title: A Next.js developer needs an environment variable to be accessible in client-side JavaScript. What naming convention is required?
questions.prompt: A Next.js developer needs an environment variable to be accessible in client-side JavaScript. What naming convention is required?

options.text: `REACT_APP_API_KEY`
`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_KEY`
`PUBLIC_API_KEY`
`CLIENT_API_KEY`

questions.explanation: Next.js only inlines environment variables into the browser bundle when they are prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. All other env variables remain server-side only and are never included in client code, protecting secrets like database passwords and API tokens from exposure.

questions.title: A developer wants a statically generated page to automatically refresh stale content every 10 minutes without a full rebuild. What is the correct approach?
questions.prompt: A developer wants a statically generated page to automatically refresh stale content every 10 minutes without a full rebuild. What is the correct approach?

options.text: This is incorrect; use `getServerSideProps` instead for refreshing content
This uses Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) — after 600 seconds, the next request triggers background regeneration while the stale page is served
The page is rebuilt every 600 seconds automatically regardless of traffic
`revalidate` is not a valid key in the `getStaticProps` return object

questions.explanation: ISR combines the performance of static pages with the freshness of server rendering. Once the revalidation window expires, the next visitor gets the stale page immediately while Next.js regenerates it in the background. The freshly generated page replaces the old one for subsequent visitors.

questions.title: In Next.js App Router (`app/` directory), what is the role of a `layout.tsx` file?
questions.prompt: In Next.js App Router (`app/` directory), what is the role of a `layout.tsx` file?

options.text: It defines page-level `<head>` metadata like `<title>` and Open Graph tags
It is a persistent UI shell that wraps the current segment and all nested segments, preserving state across route changes
It replaces `getServerSideProps` for server-side data fetching
It is used only for CSS-in-JS scope isolation

questions.explanation: `layout.tsx` defines shared UI (nav, sidebar, providers) that persists across navigations within its segment. React preserves the layout component\'s state and DOM — it is not unmounted when a child route changes. Every segment can have its own `layout.tsx`, and they nest automatically for granular control.

questions.title: In Next.js App Router, what does adding `"use client"` at the top of a file declare?
questions.prompt: In Next.js App Router, what does adding `"use client"` at the top of a file declare?

options.text: The file should only be included in the development bundle
The component is a Client Component — it is hydrated in the browser and can use hooks, state, and browser APIs
The file handles client authentication logic only
All exports from the file are server-only utilities

questions.explanation: By default, all App Router components are React Server Components that render only on the server with zero JavaScript shipped to the client. Adding `"use client"` marks a boundary: that file and its imports become part of the client bundle, enabling interactivity via `useState`, `useEffect`, and event handlers. Server Components cannot use these APIs.

questions.title: A developer uses `getStaticPaths` with `fallback: 'blocking'`. What happens when a visitor requests a path that was not pre-generated at build time?
questions.prompt: A developer uses `getStaticPaths` with `fallback: 'blocking'`. What happens when a visitor requests a path that was not pre-generated at build time?

options.text: A 404 page is returned immediately
A loading skeleton from `router.isFallback` is shown while the page generates
The page is server-rendered on the first request, the response is cached as static HTML, and subsequent visitors get the static file
The Next.js build is triggered again to include the new path

questions.explanation: `fallback: 'blocking'` generates unbuilt pages on-demand via SSR (the request blocks until rendering is complete), then stores the result as static HTML. Unlike `fallback: true`, no intermediate loading state is shown. Use it when you want on-demand generation without a loading flash.

questions.title: Where does Next.js Middleware execute, and what is it primarily used for?
questions.prompt: Where does Next.js Middleware execute, and what is it primarily used for?

options.text: In the browser after the page loads, to modify the DOM
In the Node.js API runtime to validate request bodies
At the Edge runtime, before a request is matched to a route — for redirects, rewrites, auth checks, and header manipulation
Inside React Server Components as an async data-fetching wrapper

questions.explanation: Next.js Middleware runs in the lightweight Edge Runtime (V8-based) and executes before route resolution. It is ideal for authentication redirects, A/B testing, geo-targeting, and request/response header manipulation with near-zero added latency since it runs at the network edge close to the user.

questions.title: In the Next.js App Router, what is the purpose of `generateStaticParams`?
questions.prompt: In the Next.js App Router, what is the purpose of `generateStaticParams`?

options.text: It validates the params passed to a dynamic route at runtime
It is the App Router equivalent of `getStaticPaths` — it returns param objects to pre-render at build time
It generates TypeScript types for dynamic route parameters
It runs on every request to fetch the latest parameters from the database

questions.explanation: `generateStaticParams` replaces `getStaticPaths` from the Pages Router. It is exported from a dynamic segment\'s `page.tsx` and returns an array of param objects that Next.js uses to determine which paths to pre-render during `next build`.

questions.title: In the Next.js App Router, how do React Server Components (RSC) fetch data differently from client components?
questions.prompt: In the Next.js App Router, how do React Server Components (RSC) fetch data differently from client components?

options.text: RSC use `useEffect` with `fetch` in the component body
RSC use a special `getData()` hook provided by Next.js
RSC can be declared as `async` functions and `await` data directly in the component body — no hooks required
RSC require Redux Toolkit for all server-side data fetching

questions.explanation: React Server Components run exclusively on the server and are never hydrated in the browser. Because they do not participate in the React hook lifecycle, they can be `async` functions that `await` database queries, file reads, or API calls directly in the component body, eliminating the need for `useEffect`-based data fetching patterns.

questions.title: A developer wraps a slow data-fetching Server Component with `<Suspense>` in the Next.js App Router. What is the performance benefit?
questions.prompt: A developer wraps a slow data-fetching Server Component with `<Suspense>` in the Next.js App Router. What is the performance benefit?

content.value:
<Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
  <SlowDataComponent />
</Suspense>

options.text: It moves `SlowDataComponent` to client-side rendering automatically
It enables HTML streaming — the server sends the outer shell (including the fallback) immediately and streams the component\'s HTML when its data resolves
It caches the component\'s output in a Redis store
It prevents `SlowDataComponent` from receiving any props until data is ready

questions.explanation: Next.js App Router supports HTTP streaming via React Suspense. The server flushes the page shell and Suspense fallback to the browser immediately (improving TTFB), then streams the resolved component HTML as a small `<script>` injection once the awaited data is ready — without a full page reload or client-side fetch.

questions.title: A developer sets up React Router v6. Which component provides the routing context to the entire application?
questions.prompt: A developer sets up React Router v6. Which component provides the routing context to the entire application?

options.text: `<Routes>`
`<Route>`
`<BrowserRouter>`
`<Switch>`

questions.explanation: `<BrowserRouter>` provides the routing context to the component tree using the browser\'s History API. `<Routes>` selects the best-matching `<Route>` for the current URL. `<Switch>` was the v5 equivalent of `<Routes>` and does not exist in v6.

questions.title: A developer needs to read the `:id` parameter from the URL `/users/42`. Which React Router v6 hook should they use?
questions.prompt: A developer needs to read the `:id` parameter from the URL `/users/42`. Which React Router v6 hook should they use?

options.text: `useQuery()`
`useHistory()`
`useParams()`
`useLocation()`

questions.explanation: `useParams()` returns an object of the matched URL parameters. For a route defined as `/users/:id`, calling `const { id } = useParams()` gives `"42"`. `useHistory` was the v5 API replaced by `useNavigate` in v6. `useLocation` provides the current location object (pathname, search, hash) without URL params.

questions.title: A developer wants to programmatically redirect to `/dashboard` after a successful form submission. Which React Router v6 hook should they use?
questions.prompt: A developer wants to programmatically redirect to `/dashboard` after a successful form submission. Which React Router v6 hook should they use?

options.text: `useHistory()`
`useNavigate()`
`useLocation()`
`useRedirect()`

questions.explanation: In React Router v6, `useNavigate()` returns a `navigate` function for imperative navigation: `const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/dashboard")`. `useHistory()` was its v5 predecessor and was removed in v6. `useLocation()` only reads the current URL without navigating.

questions.title: A developer builds a protected route pattern. What does the following component do?
questions.prompt: A developer builds a protected route pattern. What does the following component do?

options.text: It always renders children and ignores the auth state
It renders children when authenticated; otherwise it declaratively redirects to `/login` using `<Navigate>`
It suspends rendering until authentication resolves
`<Navigate>` is only valid as a direct child of `<Routes>`

questions.explanation: `<Navigate>` is the declarative redirect component in React Router v6. When rendered, it immediately triggers a navigation to the specified route. The `replace` prop replaces the current history entry so the user cannot navigate back to the protected page with the browser back button.

questions.title: A developer defines nested routes in React Router v6. Where must `<Outlet />` be placed for child routes to render?
questions.prompt: A developer defines nested routes in React Router v6. Where must `<Outlet />` be placed for child routes to render?

content.value:
<Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
  <Route path="stats" element={<Stats />} />
  <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
</Route>

options.text: In each of the child components (`<Stats />`, `<Settings />`)
In `<DashboardLayout />`, at the position where the matched child route element should appear
Immediately inside `<BrowserRouter>`
`<Outlet />` is not needed; child routes render automatically

questions.explanation: `<Outlet>` is a placeholder inside a parent route\'s element component. It renders the matched child route\'s element at that position. Without `<Outlet>`, child routes match in the URL but their elements never appear in the DOM.
